result: behaviorMate is an integrated system using networked hardware and software components that communicate via JSON-formatted UDP packets on a LAN. The system includes a Java-based UI, Behavior Controller (Arduino Due with custom PCB), and Position Controller (Arduino Nano with quadrature decoder) with specific technical specifications for timing, GPIO control, and position tracking.
evaluation: Claims C1-C75 provide comprehensive technical documentation of the system architecture. The hardware specifications, communication protocols, and software design patterns are explicitly described with sufficient detail for replication. The modular design using standard protocols (UDP, JSON) is well-justified and technically sound.

result: behaviorMate provides a cost-effective alternative to proprietary systems, with total costs of approximately $3700 for VR rigs and $1700 for treadmill systems, using exclusively open-source software without requiring users to write code.
evaluation: Claims C5-C6 provide specific cost estimates that are reasonable given the listed components. Claims C50-C53 accurately characterize the open-source nature and compare to proprietary alternatives (C51). The cost advantage and accessibility claims are well-supported, though C51's characterization of proprietary system costs lacks specific citations.

result: Treadmill position tracking accuracy was validated with mean lap time error of 0.102 seconds and mean position error of 13 mm (max 23 mm) compared to computer vision ground truth. A lap-reset feature prevents drift accumulation.
evaluation: Claims C18-C19 report quantitative benchmarking with appropriate methodology (C85 - OpenCV for ground truth). The errors are small relative to typical reward zone sizes and mouse dimensions. C83-C84 acknowledge limitations and provide the lap-reset solution. The validation approach is sound and results demonstrate acceptable accuracy.

result: VR system latency between wheel movement and screen update had a median of 0.067 seconds (max 0.087 s), which is below mouse reaction time (~0.1 s). Position tracking accuracy showed mean error of 4.1 mm compared to ground truth.
evaluation: Claims C24 and C26 provide quantitative benchmarking data with appropriate sample sizes (n=20 for latency). C25 cites published literature for mouse reaction times to contextualize the latency measurements. The validation demonstrates the VR system performs within biologically relevant timescales. Methodology using high-speed camera and computer vision is appropriate.

result: The VR system uses Unity/C# (VRMate) with distributed rendering on separate Android devices (ODROID C4) for each display, achieving scalability without compromising frame rate. The standard setup uses five monitors at 135-degree angles in an octagonal configuration, with custom shader support for removing color channels to minimize imaging artifacts.
evaluation: Claims C20-C23, C95-C104 describe the VR architecture comprehensively. The distributed rendering approach (C96, C100-C101) is technically sound for achieving scalability. Hardware specifications are detailed (C21). The shader capability (C103-C104) addresses a practical concern for fluorescence imaging. The design is well-justified and technically appropriate.

result: Experimental validation used six adult mice (3 male, 3 female, 8-16 weeks) with jGCaMP8m injections in dorsal CA1, following standard surgical and training protocols. Two-photon imaging was performed using an 8-kHz resonant scanner with 16× objective at 920 nm excitation, recording an average of 1533±481 neurons in VR and 1057±169 neurons in TM.
evaluation: Claims C28-C140 provide comprehensive methodological details for the experimental validation. Sample size (n=6) is modest but reasonable for imaging studies. Sex balance (C29) is appropriate. Surgical procedures, imaging parameters, and training protocols are standard and well-described. IACUC approval is documented (C125). The methods are reproducible and follow established practices.

result: Calcium imaging data were processed using Suite2p for motion correction and ROI detection, with OASIS for spike inference. Binarized event trains (threshold: 4 MAD) were used for all analyses. Place cells were identified using circular shuffle statistics (99th percentile, 1000 shuffles) with spatial criteria (3-25 consecutive significant bins, 50% trial consistency).
evaluation: Claims C122-C157 describe standard and appropriate analysis methods for calcium imaging. Software tools (Suite2p, OASIS) are well-established and properly cited. The place cell classification criteria (C148-C151) are rigorous with appropriate statistical controls. C146 appropriately disclaims that binarized signals represent true spiking. The analysis pipeline is reproducible and follows field standards.

result: VR had significantly fewer CA1 neurons classified as place cells (34.9%, 3253/9195) compared to TM (44.9%, 6101/13,454; z=14.96, p=1.27e-50), but place cells tiled the entire track in both environments.
evaluation: Claims C35-C36 report a statistically significant difference in place cell proportions with appropriate statistical test (two-sample z-test) and large sample sizes. The p-value is extremely significant. Despite the difference in proportions, both systems show complete spatial coverage (C36), which is the key functional validation. The finding is consistent with prior literature cited in C43.

result: Two-way repeated measures ANOVA revealed no significant effects of environment (VR vs. TM) or context (familiar vs. novel) on mean ΔF/F amplitude (environment: F(1,5)=1.94, p=0.222; context: F(1,5)=0.004, p=0.954), frequency (environment: F(1,5)=4.38, p=0.091; context: F(1,5)=0.079, p=0.790), or spatial information (environment: F(1,5)=0.74, p=0.43; context: F(1,5)=3.79, p=0.11).
evaluation: Claims C37-C38, C42 report appropriate statistical analyses (two-way repeated measures ANOVA) with complete reporting of F-statistics, degrees of freedom, and p-values. The lack of significant effects on these measures suggests similar calcium transient properties across conditions. However, the sample size (n=6 mice, df=5) is modest, which may limit statistical power to detect smaller effects. The results are internally consistent.

result: Two-way ANOVA revealed significant effects of environment on place cell sensitivity (F(1,5)=9.85, p=0.0257) and specificity (F(1,5)=53.32, p=0.0008), with TM place cells showing higher trial-by-trial in-field firing compared to VR. No significant context effects were observed.
evaluation: Claims C39-C40 report statistically significant environment effects with appropriate tests and complete statistics. The specificity effect (p=0.0008) is highly significant despite modest sample size. C41 provides a reasonable interpretation of these findings. The results are consistent with prior literature (C43) showing reduced trial-by-trial reliability in VR while maintaining spatial information encoding.

result: The observed differences in VR and TM place cell properties are consistent with previous findings of reduced trial-by-trial reliability in VR, potentially due to absence of proximal visual and tactile cues during VR tasks.
evaluation: Claims C43-C44 appropriately contextualize the findings within existing literature (citing Ravassard et al., 2013; Aghajan et al., 2015; Dombeck et al., 2010; Aronov and Tank, 2014; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Priestley et al., 2022). The interpretation regarding cue salience (C44) is speculative but reasonable and supported by cited literature (Knierim and Rao, 2003; Renaudineau et al., 2007; Sofroniew et al., 2014).

result: Place cells remapped when exposed to novel contexts in both VR and TM. Bayesian decoders trained on familiar trials decoded held-out familiar trials significantly above chance (p<0.05) but performed at chance level when tested on novel trials, demonstrating context-dependent remapping in both environments.
evaluation: Claims C45-C49 describe remapping observations with appropriate statistical validation using Bayesian decoding (C160, citing Zhang et al., 1998). The cross-validation approach (C163) is appropriate. Subsampling to match cell numbers (C164) controls for a potential confound. The chance level calculations (C161-C162) are reasonable, though the TM method (track length/4) could be better justified. The finding that decoders fail on novel contexts demonstrates genuine remapping rather than drift.

result: behaviorMate has been successfully used in numerous published studies for diverse experimental paradigms including head-fixed navigation with two-photon microscopy, trace fear conditioning, goal-oriented learning, context switching, optogenetic stimulation, and investigation of synaptic plasticity mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C27, C76-C77, C86-C90, C118-C121 cite extensive published literature demonstrating the system's utility across multiple experimental paradigms and laboratories. The citations span 2016-2023 and include high-impact findings (e.g., C90 - first optical induction of place fields). This provides strong validation of the system's reliability and versatility, though it represents prior work rather than new findings in this manuscript.

result: Head-restrained setups with treadmills and VR systems have been widely used to study navigation, with spatial representations from freely moving animals largely conserved. Place cells, grid cells, and other spatial tuning properties have been observed in both belt-based and VR systems across hippocampal subregions and entorhinal cortex.
evaluation: Claims C8-C10, C54-C59, C91-C94 provide appropriate background context citing relevant literature. These are well-established findings in the field and the citations are appropriate. However, these represent prior work and general knowledge rather than new contributions. The claims accurately summarize the state of the field and justify the experimental approach.

result: The treadmill and VR systems incorporate specific design features optimized for imaging: belt construction from fabric ribbon with physical cues, vibration-absorbing design without platform beneath the mouse, goniometers for head angle adjustment, lightweight running wheel with low rotational momentum, and light-blocking head restraining bars.
evaluation: Claims C78-C82, C105-C107, C112-C117 describe practical design features with clear functional justifications. The vibration-absorbing design (C79) and goniometer positioning (C80, C117) are well-justified for imaging applications. The lightweight wheel design (C112-C113) cites Warren et al., 2021. These are reasonable engineering solutions, though some claims (e.g., C79, C82, C113) involve functional inferences that could benefit from quantitative validation.

result: The VR system supports rapid visual context switches, addition of novel virtual objects, and hybrid setups combining visual displays with physical treadmills. Alternative configurations include wireless tablet-based setups (5 Fire HD 10 tablets) for space-constrained environments using static IP assignment via router configuration.
evaluation: Claims C97-C98 describe system capabilities that are logical extensions of the architecture. Claims C108-C111 provide specific details for an alternative tablet-based configuration with complete hardware specifications and networking setup. The flexibility claims are reasonable given the modular design, though actual implementation of hybrid setups is not demonstrated in the validation experiments.
